h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: Replacing a weak pooling op on the final edge into the output gives a larger gain than replacing other ops, including conv3x3 itself which yields zero change.
Discarding the strongest op on edge 1 makes the pooling edit far more harmful than replacing a weaker op.
Cutting node 1 off costs the most when the removed edge carried the strongest operation.
With edge 0 none, node 1 is all zeros, so a conv on edge 2 processes nothing and its usual gain disappears.
With node 1 empty, edge 4 cannot carry useful signal to the output, so the conv's usual gain vanishes.
With edge 5 none, node 2 is disconnected from the output, so upgrading edge 1 cannot affect accuracy.
With node 2 disconnected from the output, the usually harmful pooling edit on edge 2 has no effect.
Pooling an all-zero node 1 contributes nothing, so the usual harm of the edit vanishes.
With edge 4 already none, removing edge 5 leaves only the edge-3 shortcut feeding the output, collapsing the cell far more than when edge 4 offers an alternate path.
With edge 2 none, node 2 depends solely on edge 1, so upgrading it to conv3x3 drives the whole node-2 branch and yields a larger gain.
